reviewMethod.methodNotesMd: I reviewed the resource-level contract, rubric, fresh-review framework, the CatalogEntry structure report, the resource-review context, the deterministic aggregate, the R4 CatalogEntry StructureDefinition, the R6 catalog-related package index/profile evidence, and the direct REST behavior finding. Shared Resource/DomainResource behavior findings were considered only as context because the reviewed artifact is CatalogEntry, not Resource or DomainResource.

r4Maturity.effectMd: R4 CatalogEntry was trial-use/FMM 0, so the standards-stability burden is weak compared with mature or normative resources. That softens the case for preserving a deprecated core resource, but it does not erase practical catalog/orderability risk for implementers that used the wrapper in production.

overall.oneLineConclusion: CatalogEntry is removed from R6 core, so R4 instances require a resource-level migration program; further compatibility value is mainly in explicit migration guidance rather than preserving individual old elements.

reasoning.thesisMd: `CatalogEntry` is not a mostly stable resource with a few local breaks. R4 defined it as a concrete `DomainResource`, but the supplied R6 core package has no CatalogEntry StructureDefinition and lists the name only as an old type. Any R4 instance with `resourceType: "CatalogEntry"` therefore fails before element-level preservation can help.
reasoning.migrationShapeMd: The migration shape is resource retirement/replacement, not a path rename. R4 CatalogEntry carried mandatory per-item facts such as `orderable` and `referencedItem`, plus status, validity, identifiers, classifications, characteristics, and optional `relatedEntry` self-links. R6 retains catalog infrastructure through a `catalog` profile on `Composition`, but that profile already existed in R4 and is not a same-shape per-entry carrier. Implementers must choose a new modeling pattern: move metadata to the referenced item, use a catalog Composition/profile, define extensions, or preserve an implementation-specific compatibility wrapper.
reasoning.compatibilityLeverageMd: Because the resource identity is gone, keeping an individual field name or relation code would not by itself let R4 instances validate as R6. A deprecated compatibility resource and old endpoint aliases would be the true base-compatible option, but that is a broad ongoing support commitment for FMM 0 content and may create duplicate catalog representations. This makes migration-program planning the dominant lever. The remaining break-prevention value is still real, but it is concentrated in low-cost guidance, mappings, and transition metadata rather than in field-by-field base preservation.
reasoning.lessBreakingAlternativesMd: The strongest less-breaking base design would have kept CatalogEntry as a deprecated R6 compatibility resource, including `relatedEntry` and the old relation-type terminology. That would preserve many R4 instances, but it is not a small local fix: validators, SDKs, servers, CapabilityStatements, and search/REST surfaces would all continue to support an obsolete wrapper. Lower-cost actions are more proportionate here: an official migration table or ConceptMap, guidance for mapping `orderable`, `referencedItem`, status/validity/classification, and relationship code semantics, and a clear statement about whether Composition catalog profiles or item-specific profiles are intended successors.
reasoning.behaviorImpactMd: The direct HTTP behavior finding matters for CatalogEntry because the R4 base CapabilityStatement advertised a CatalogEntry REST endpoint and R6 no longer does. For this resource, however, that endpoint loss is derivative of the resource removal rather than an independent redesign: an endpoint alias is only useful if a compatibility resource or transform contract also exists. The eleven shared Resource/DomainResource behavior findings remain background compatibility context and were not scored as CatalogEntry-specific drivers.
reasoning.comparisonToDeterministicAggregateMd: I agree with the deterministic aggregate's main result: major migration is unavoidable, the migration shape is `removed-or-replaced-resource`, and resource-level compatibility leverage is best described as `migration-program-dominates`. My qualification is that this should not be read as saying the local metadata and relationship semantics are unimportant; they are important migration-map content and standards-review topics, even if preserving the old resource in base R6 is not a low-cost compatibility tweak.
reasoning.uncertaintyMd: The package evidence is strong that CatalogEntry is absent in R6 ballot4, but the supplied files do not include an official retirement rationale, successor-resource decision, ConceptMap, or final-release confirmation. Production prevalence is also unknown.

findingConsiderations.title: CatalogEntry resource is absent from the R6 core package
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is the controlling finding. With no same-name R6 StructureDefinition, R4 CatalogEntry instances are old-valid/new-invalid at the resource identity level, and generated R6 SDKs, validators, server route inventories, and resource-type switches will not expose a normal CatalogEntry surface.

findingConsiderations.title: CatalogEntry's per-item wrapper metadata has no direct R6 resource carrier
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This finding shows why the resource removal is a real model migration rather than a simple delete. R4 CatalogEntry carried business-relevant item metadata such as orderability, referenced item, status, validity, identifiers, classifications, and characteristics. These facts need an explicit destination in any R6 migration pattern.

findingConsiderations.title: CatalogEntry related-entry graph and relation-type terminology are not preserved in R6 core
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The optional related-entry graph is not what makes migration unavoidable, but it is a meaningful local migration chore for catalogs that used `triggers` or `is-replaced-by` relationships. It deserves mapping guidance because generic Composition relationships do not obviously preserve the same per-entry semantics.

findingConsiderations.title: The full base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises many R4 resource REST endpoints
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: CatalogEntry is one of the affected endpoint types. The REST/API break is concrete for discovery-driven clients, but for CatalogEntry it follows from the removed resource identity; endpoint preservation would require a compatibility resource, an alias-and-transform contract, or explicit replacement guidance.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 core removes the Resource $meta operation
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This Resource-level operation change may affect servers that also host CatalogEntry compatibility surfaces, but it is not specific to CatalogEntry and should not drive the CatalogEntry resource-level migration conclusion.

findingConsiderations.title: Core special/profile search parameters changed type metadata for _content, _text, _query, and _profile
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The shared search-parameter metadata change is relevant background for cross-version clients, but it is inherited infrastructure behavior, not a CatalogEntry-specific model or endpoint decision.

recommendedNextActions.actionMd: Publish explicit CatalogEntry retirement guidance that maps R4 wrapper fields, especially `orderable`, `referencedItem`, status, validity, identifiers, classifications, and characteristics, to the intended R6 resources, profiles, or extensions.
Define relationship migration guidance for `CatalogEntry.relatedEntry`, including how `triggers` and `is-replaced-by` should be represented or intentionally retired in R6 catalog models.

Clarify the REST transition story for CatalogEntry: whether implementations should expose no R6 endpoint, a deprecated compatibility endpoint, an alias with transform behavior, or only successor-resource endpoints.
Re-run the assessment against the final R6 package or any official migration artifacts, because the current evidence is based on the supplied R6 ballot4 package.

caveats: The supplied R6 input is 6.0.0-ballot4 rather than a final R6 publication.
No official CatalogEntry retirement rationale, ConceptMap, or field-level migration table was present in the supplied package files.
CatalogEntry production prevalence is unknown; R4 FMM 0 weakens stability pressure but does not prove no systems used it.
Shared Resource and DomainResource behavior findings were treated as context only, per the resource-review instructions.
